facts.statement: The animal belongs to the genus Europasaurus.
facts.quote: genus: Europasaurus

facts.statement: The species name of the animal is holgeri.
facts.quote: species: holgeri

facts.statement: The genus was described by Mateus et al. in Sander et al., 2006.
facts.quote: parent_authority: Mateus et al. in Sander et al., 2006

facts.statement: Europasaurus lived in northern Germany during the Late Jurassic, specifically the middle Kimmeridgian stage, between 154 and 151 million years ago.
facts.quote: It lived during the Late Jurassic (middle Kimmeridgian, from about 154 to 151 million years ago) of northern Germany

facts.statement: A single sauropod tooth was discovered in 1998 by private fossil collector Holger Lüdtke.
facts.quote: In 1998, a single sauropod tooth was discovered by private fossil collector Holger Lüdtke

facts.statement: The taxon was formally described as Europasaurus holgeri in 2006.
facts.quote: In 2006, the new sauropod taxon was formally described as Europasaurus holgeri

facts.statement: The specific name 'holgeri' honors Holger Lüdtke, who discovered the first fossils.
facts.quote: the specific name honours Holger Lüdtke, the discoverer of the first fossils

facts.statement: A partial sauropod skull, the first of its kind discovered in Europe, was revealed in January 2002.
facts.quote: By January 2002, preparation of an even larger block had revealed a partial sauropod skull – the first to be discovered in Europe

facts.statement: Part of the fossil material was damaged or destroyed by an arson fire on the night of October 4–5, 2003.
facts.quote: Part of the Europasaurus fossil material got damaged or destroyed by arson fire on the night of 4–5 October 2003

facts.statement: The holotype selected was a disarticulated but associated individual designated DFMMh/FV 291.
facts.quote: From these specimens, the holotype was selected, a disarticulated but associated individual (DFMMh/FV 291)

facts.statement: As an adult, Europasaurus measured 5.7 to 6.2 meters long and weighed between 750 and 2100 kilograms.
facts.quote: Europasaurus is a very small sauropod, measuring only 5.7 - 6.2 m long and weighed 750 - 2100 kg as an adult

facts.statement: Younger individuals are known, ranging from 3.7 meters in length down to the youngest juvenile at 1.75 meters.
facts.quote: Younger individuals are known, from sizes of 3.7 m to the youngest juvenile at 1.75 m

facts.statement: Europasaurus has a shorter snout compared to Brachiosaurus.
facts.quote: Europasaurus has a shorter snout

facts.statement: It was initially assumed that the small bones belonged to juveniles, but the 2006 publication established that most specimens were adults and that the species exhibited insular dwarfism.
facts.quote: Given the comparatively small size of the bones, it was initially assumed that they stem from juvenile individuals. The 2006 publication, however, established that the majority of specimens were adult, and that Europasaurus was an island dwarf

facts.statement: Most external skull bones of Europasaurus are preserved, except for the prefrontals.
facts.quote: Nearly all external skull bones have been preserved among Europasaurus specimens, except the prefrontals.

facts.statement: Eight premaxillae of Europasaurus have been found, showing a rectangular snout shape similar to Camarasaurus.
facts.quote: Eight premaxillae are known, with a generally rectangular snout shape as found in Camarasaurus.

facts.statement: Europasaurus had approximately 12 to 13 teeth in its maxilla, a number lower than in basal taxa but within the range seen in Brachiosauridae.
facts.quote: There were about 12–13 total teeth in the maxilla of Europasaurus, fewer than in more basal taxa (16 teeth in Jobaria and 14–25 in Atlasaurus), but falling within the range of variation in Brachiosauridae (15 in Brachiosaurus to 10 in Abydosaurus).

facts.statement: Four frontal bones of Europasaurus are known, consisting of three from the left side and one from the right.
facts.quote: Four frontals are known from Europasaurus, three being from the left and one being from the right.

facts.statement: The frontals of Europasaurus likely never fused during growth due to their disarticulated state, unlike in Camarasaurus.
facts.quote: Because of their disarticulation, it is likely that the frontals never fused during growth, unlike in Camarasaurus.

facts.statement: Several parietal bones of Europasaurus are known, exhibiting a rectangular shape that is much wider than long.
facts.quote: Several parietal bones are known in Europasaurus, which show a rectangular shape much wider than long.

facts.statement: The parietals of Europasaurus possess a postparietal fenestra, a feature rarely found outside of Dicraeosauridae.
facts.quote: Besides the before mentioned fenestra, the parietals also have a "postparietal fenestra", something rarely seen outside of Dicraeosauridae.

facts.statement: Multiple jugal bones of Europasaurus are known, showing a morphology more similar to basal sauropodomorphs than other macronarians.
facts.quote: Multiple jugals are known from Europasaurus, which are more similar in morphology to basal sauropodomorphs than other macronarians.

facts.statement: The two processes of the quadratojugal bone in Europasaurus diverge at nearly 90 degrees, with the dorsal process curving to follow the shape of the quadrate.
facts.quote: The two quadratojugal processes diverge at a nearly right angle (90º), although the dorsal process curves as it follows the shape of the quadrate.

facts.statement: Squamosal bones of Europasaurus have a question-mark shape in lateral view, similar to those of Camarasaurus.
facts.quote: Squamosals found from Europasaurus show the same approximate shape in lateral view as Camarasaurus, that of a question mark.

facts.statement: Thirteen elements of the palate of Europasaurus are preserved, including the quadrate, pterygoid, and ectopterygoid.
facts.quote: There are thirteen preserved elements of the palate of Europasaurus, including the quadrate, pterygoid and ectopterygoid.

facts.statement: The pterygoid bones of Europasaurus are the largest in the sauropod palate and have a triradiate shape similar to the postorbitals.
facts.quote: Pterygoids are the largest of the sauropod palate bones, and it has a triradiate shape, like the postorbitals.

facts.statement: Adult cervical vertebrae of Europasaurus are elongated and opisthocoelous with a notch on the rear end.
facts.quote: The adult cervical centra are elongated and opisthocoelous (anterior end is ball-shaped), with a notch in the top of the rear end of the centrum.

facts.statement: The sides of Europasaurus cervical centra have an excavation opening into internal pneumaticity.
facts.quote: In the side of the centra of Europasaurus there is an excavation which opens into the internal pneumaticity of the vertebrae.

facts.statement: Unlike Giraffatitan and other brachiosaurids, Europasaurus lacks thin ridges dividing the pneumatic opening in its vertebrae.
facts.quote: Unlike in Giraffatitan and brachiosaurids, Europasaurus does not have thin ridges (laminae) dividing this opening.

facts.statement: Fossilized skin impressions of Europasaurus relatives show several types of scales but no bony plates or nodules indicating armor.
facts.quote: There are no bony plates or nodules, to indicate armour, but there are several types of scales.

facts.statement: Initially, Europasaurus was classified within Macronaria but outside the families Brachiosauridae and the clade Titanosauromorpha.
facts.quote: When it was first named, Europasaurus was considered to be a taxon within Macronaria that didn't fall within the family Brachiosauridae or the clade Titanosauromorpha.

facts.statement: A 2012 analysis by D'Emic considered Europasaurus to belong within Brachiosauridae rather than being basal to the group.
facts.quote: In a 2012 analysis of the phylogeny of Titanosauriformes, D'Emic (2012) considered Europasaurus to belong to Brachiosauridae, instead of being basal to the earliest brachiosaurids.

facts.statement: Despite strong phylogenetic support, Europasaurus lacks several characteristic bones of Brachiosauridae, such as caudal vertebrae, making its placement tentative.
facts.quote: While there was strong support in the phylogeny for its placement, Europasaurus, one of few basal macronarians with a skull, lacks multiple bones that display characteristic features of the group, such as caudal vertebrae.

facts.statement: A 2017 phylogeny by Royo-Torres et al. resolved complex relationships within Brachiosauridae, placing Europasaurus as the basalmost member.
facts.quote: A 2017 phylogeny, that of Royo-Torres et al. (2017), resolved more complex relations within Brachiosauridae.

facts.statement: Histology analysis confirmed that Europasaurus was a unique dwarf species rather than a juvenile of another taxon like Camarasaurus.
facts.quote: It was identified that Europasaurus was a unique dwarf species, and not a juvenile of an existing taxon like Camarasaurus, by a histology analysis of multiple specimens of Europasaurus.

facts.statement: The smallest known specimen of Europasaurus measured 1.75 meters in length.
facts.quote: The youngest specimen (DFMMh/FV 009) was shown by this analysis to lack signs of aging such as growth marks or laminar bone tissue, and is also the smallest specimen at 1.75 m in length.

facts.statement: A juvenile specimen of Europasaurus measured 2 meters in length.
facts.quote: A larger specimen (DFMMh/FV 291.9) at 2 m shows large amounts of laminar tissue, with no growth marks present, so is likely a juvenile as well.

facts.statement: A subadult specimen of Europasaurus measured 3.5 meters in length.
facts.quote: The next smallest specimen (DFMMh/FV 001) has shows the presence of growth marks (specifically annuli), and at the length of 3.5 m is possibly a subadult.

facts.statement: A specimen of Europasaurus measuring 3.7 meters displayed mature osteons and annuli.
facts.quote: Further larger, DFMMh/FV 495 displays mature osteons as well as annuli, and is 3.7 m.

facts.statement: The second largest analyzed specimen of Europasaurus measured 4.2 meters in length.
facts.quote: The second largest analysed specimen (DFMMh/FV 153) also shows growth marks, but they are more frequent. This specimen is 4.2 m.

facts.statement: The largest known individual of Europasaurus reached a body length of 6.2 meters.
facts.quote: A single partial femur represents the largest known Europasaurus individual, at a body length of 6.2 m.

facts.statement: Europasaurus developed its small size due to a significantly reduced growth rate compared to larger taxa like Camarasaurus.
facts.quote: These combinations of growth factors show that Europasaurus developed its small size because of a largely reduced growth rate, gaining size slower than larger taxa such as Camarasaurus.

facts.statement: Researchers proposed that the small size of Europasaurus resulted from pedomorphism, where adults retained juvenile characteristics.
facts.quote: Marpmann et al. (2014) proposed that the small size and reduced growth rate of Europasaurus was an effect of pedomorphism, where the adults of taxa retain juvenile characteristics, such as size.

facts.statement: Infant Europasaurus were likely precocial but relied on adult protection within herds, a behavior not seen in larger sauropods.
facts.quote: Examinations of the inner ears of infant Europasaurus suggest they were precocial, and it is suggested that they would have been reliant on the protections of adults in a herd to some degree, something not seen in larger sauropods due to the massive size difference in parent and offspring.

facts.statement: The long inner ears of Europasaurus suggest they had good hearing and displayed gregarious behavior for intraspecific communication.
facts.quote: The structure and long length of the inner ear in this genus also suggests that they had good senses of hearing, with Europasaurus. Intraspecific communication was also apparently important to this sauropod, based on these studies, suggesting this sauropod displayed clear, gregarious behavior.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Europasaurus evolved its small size through island dwarfism after migrating to an island smaller than 200,000 square kilometers.
facts.quote: It has been suggested that an ancestor of Europasaurus would have quickly decreased in body size after emigrating to an island that existed at the time, as the largest of the islands in the region around northern Germany was smaller than 200000 km squared, which may not have been able to support a community of large sauropods.

facts.statement: An alternative hypothesis suggests Europasaurus shrank in size while living on a large landmass rather than an island.
facts.quote: Alternately, a macronarian may have shrunken concurrently with a larger landmass, until achieving the size of Europasaurus.

facts.statement: Europasaurus belongs to the parent group Camarasauromorpha.
facts.quote: Parent group: Camarasauromorpha

facts.statement: Europasaurus is classified in the class Saurischia.
facts.quote: Class: Saurischia

facts.statement: The type species of the genus Europasaurus is Europasaurus holgeri.
facts.quote: Type species: Europasaurus holgeri

facts.statement: Europasaurus lived during the Kimmeridgian stage, between 152.21 and 149.2 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Kimmeridgian to Kimmeridgian (152.21 to 149.2 million years ago)
